podcast.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (1973)
podcast.body: On July 2nd, 1973, after David Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon Theatre in London, a young Steve Jones managed to get inside the building and steal microphones and amps. These stolen items would later be used by Jones to start his new band, the Sex Pistols, a couple of years later. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theft of Bowie's Gear (July 1973)
podcast.body: As a young thief in July 1973, Steve Jones broke into the Hammersmith Odeon during a David Bowie and The Spiders from Mars' engagement and stole microphones and amplifiers. This gear is believed to have been used by Jones and the Sex Pistols in their early rehearsals and gigs starting in 1975, initiating their contribution to the punk rock era. "a young thief named Steve Jones broke into the theatre and made off with a bunch of microphones and amplifiers."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Iggy Pop
podcast.body: Steve Jones, the ex-guitarist for the Sex Pistols, collaborated with Iggy Pop on his albums "Blah Blah Blah" (1986) and "Instinct" (1988), contributing to Iggy's career resurgence in the mid-to-late 80s. "After listening to some rough tapes of some new songs, he encouraged Iggy and his new buddy, ex-sex pistol guitar Steve Jones, to make another album."

podcast.title: Overdubbed Les Paul Sound
podcast.body: In 1977, Steve Jones of the Sex Pistols achieved a thick, heavy sound by overdubbing his Gibson Les Paul Custom approximately 20 times. This technique showcased the guitar's capability for aggressive tones in punk rock. "He's playing a Gibson Les Paul custom that has been overdubbed unto itself around 20 times to get that thick, heavy sound."

podcast.title: Played Bass on "Holidays in the Sun"
podcast.body: After Glenn Matlock's departure from The Sex Pistols, Steve Jones took on the role of playing the bass parts for the song "Holidays in the Sun." "Bass player Glenn Matlock had been fired, so it was up to Steve to play the bass parts."

xref.body: Following Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust show at the Hammersmith Odeon in London on July 2, 1973, a young thief named Steve Jones (who would later form The Sex Pistols) broke into the venue. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and managed to help himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps along with a couple of symbols."

xref.title: A&M Records Deal and Termination (1977) - Six-Day Contract
xref.body: Two months after being dropped by EMI, A&M Records signed the Sex Pistols. However, a party immediately following the signing at the label's offices resulted in significant damage, and guitarist Steve Jones was reportedly "having sex with a staffer in the bathroom." Facing questions from head office in Los Angeles and complaints from other A&M artists like The Carpenters, the label dropped the Sex Pistols after just six days, providing a buyout worth £75,000. "They were on A&M for just six days."

xref.title: Destroyed A&M Singles
xref.body: During their brief five-day tenure with A&M Records in 1977, approximately 25,000 copies of their "God Save the Queen" 7-inch single were pressed. Following their dismissal, orders were given to destroy these singles, and most were, though several dozen copies were "liberated" from the pressing plant, with some given to executives and band members like Steve Jones, who was known to sell copies. "When the pistols were fired, those singles were ordered destroyed."

xref.title: Early Gear from Bowie Theft
xref.body: When the Sex Pistols began rehearsing and performing gigs in 1975, it is presumed that some of their initial equipment, including microphones and amplifiers, was stolen from David Bowie at the Hammersmith Odeon in July 1973 by their guitarist, Steve Jones. This gear would have been part of their early contributions to the punk rock era. "And when the pistols started rehearsing and playing gigs in 1975, it is very reasonable to assume that some of the gear that they were using to kick off their contributions to the punk rock era was all stolen from Bowie in 1972."

xref.title: Early Punk Scene Figure and Guitar Teacher
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde was an American living in London at the heart of the burgeoning punk rock scene. She was a more skilled guitarist than many of her peers, even providing lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols. Her rhythm guitar style was heavily influenced by James Brown's band. "She gave lessons to novices like Steve Jones and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols."

xref.title: Influence on British Punk - Sex Pistols Connection
xref.body: Bowie's "outsider-ness," short, sharp songs, wild fashion sense, and defiant attitude endeared him to alienated working-class youth who would become the first generation of British punks. His friendships with Iggy Pop and Lou Reed (of The Velvet Underground) also made him "cool" in their eyes. Famously, on July 2nd, 1973, after Bowie's final Ziggy Stardust tour show at the Hammersmith Odeon, a young Steve Jones (later guitarist for the Sex Pistols) stole microphones and amps from the venue, gear that would be used to start his new band. "A young thief named Steve Jones somehow got inside and helped himself to whatever he could carry out, mostly some microphones and some amps."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Later Encouragement for Blah Blah Blah
xref.body: In 1985, Bowie again came to Iggy Pop's aid by listening to rough tapes of new songs and encouraging Iggy and Steve Jones to make another album, leading to "Blah Blah Blah." "In 1985, it was Bowie to the Rescue again. After listening to some rough tapes of some new songs, he encouraged Iggy and his new buddy, ex-sex pistol guitar Steve Jones, to make another album."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Activities of Members – Jones, Cook, Rotten
xref.body: After the breakup, guitarist Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook went to South America and recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten (John Liden) traveled to Jamaica to relax, immerse himself in reggae music, and smoke ganja. "Guitar Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook ended up in South America where they recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten eventually turned up in Jamaica to decompress, soak up some reggae and smoke some ganja."

xref.title: Three-Member Lineup for Recording
xref.body: For the recording of "Holidays in the Sun," The Sex Pistols were a three-piece band consisting of Johnny Rotten, Steve Jones, and Paul Cook, as bassist Glenn Matlock had been fired, requiring Steve Jones to perform the bass parts. "When the pistols recorded this next song, they were down to just three members. There was Johnny Rotten, guitarist Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook. Bass player Glenn Matlock had been fired, so it was up to Steve to play the bass parts."

xref.title: US Tour Visa Troubles
xref.body: The band faced significant difficulties obtaining working visas for their planned late 1977 American tour due to the criminal records of its members. Johnny Rotten had a minor drug charge, Steve Jones and Paul Cook had past theft charges, and Sid Vicious had a record including drug charges, assault on a police officer, attempted grand theft auto, criminal damage, and possession of a dangerous weapon. "Getting working visas for these yobbs proved to be very difficult."
